title: Explore Unit Fractions as Part of a Set
goal: I can define a set as the whole and name one or more selected objects as a fraction of it.
catchAll: Name the whole set. Count every object for the denominator and the selected objects for the numerator.

teacher.def: The denominator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are in the whole. It is the bottom part of the fraction
A unit fraction is ONE part of a whole. It always has a numerator of one.
The numerator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are being described. It is the top part of the fraction.
A fraction is a number used when a whole is split into equal parts.

glossary.whole: the one shape, unit length, complete piece or entire set named in the question
glossary.partition: divide a whole into equal parts
glossary.interval: the distance between neighboring marks on a number line

screens.title: A new kind of whole
text: Here the WHOLE is the entire collection, not one separate object.
Every object shown is a member of this one whole set.

screens.title: Count the whole set
text: Count every object once, selected or plain.
Six objects make this whole collection, so the denominator is 6.

screens.title: Select one object
text: One object is selected from the six-object whole.
The numerator is 1. The fraction is 1/6: one selected object out of six. It is a unit fraction because its numerator is 1.

screens.title: Select several objects
text: The bottom stays 6 because the whole set still has six objects. The top becomes 3: the selected fraction is 3/6. It is not a unit fraction because its numerator is 3, not 1.

screens.title: Plain objects still belong
text: The three plain objects are part of the collection too.
The denominator counts selected AND plain objects. It is not just the plain count.

screens.title: A row is not a new whole
text: These ten objects are one whole set, even though they fill more than one row.
The bottom counts all ten objects; the top counts the four selected objects.

screens.title: Positions can change
text: The selected objects may move without changing how many are selected.
If the number selected and the number in the whole set stay the same, the fraction stays the same.

screens.title: Name what is selected
text: A question may ask for unfinished tasks or plain objects instead of colored ones.
Use the prompt to decide the chosen group. For this picture the four plain objects can be the chosen group: 4/6.

sections.heading: The whole has changed
sections.text: Unlike Lesson 7-5, this lesson defines the entire collection as one whole. Ask the child to point to every member before counting a numerator or denominator.

sections.heading: Count objects, not rows
sections.text: Each object is one counting part of the collection. Selected objects still belong in the whole count. Rows, spacing and color do not create new wholes.

sections.heading: Choose the requested group
sections.text: The chosen group can be selected objects, unfinished tasks or plain objects. Read which group is requested. Both groups still belong to the denominator.

sections.heading: Scope and review
sections.text: Sets use object counts including five, ten and twelve. This lesson does not partition a collection into equal groups. The written explanation is self or parent reviewed.
